extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and practicing reporters (news reporters covering police/crime beats)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing news stories about police, crime, and related accidents: choosing story form, handling facts and moral effects, narrative treatment, fairness to accused, and the concrete details to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate story form
rubrics_metrics.description: Since police news ranges from slight misdemeanors to the most serious crimes, choose the form of story to fit the material: the purely informative story is often sufficient; strong personal elements justify an effective human-interest presentation; amusing aspects of minor offenses may warrant humorous treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use purely informative form for simple burglaries; use human-interest presentation when there is a strong personal element; use humorous treatment for minor or amusing offenses (cf. cited examples in text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of reader effect / Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: In no other kind of news should the effect of the story on the reader receive more careful consideration than in news of crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve a deterrent effect, the crime must be shown to be wrong; emphasize results of wrongdoing (legal punishment, remorse, pangs of guilty conscience, disgrace to others) so that stories tend to deter others from emulating the act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize underlying causes and responsibility when constructive
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive presentation of crime news may include emphasis on underlying causes and responsibility, especially when these can be traced to bad conditions in the community or society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such emphasis leads readers to consider the necessity for changing conditions that are directly or indirectly responsible for the criminal acts; when the criminal is a victim of circumstances it may be legitimate to create sympathetic understanding of his act (with appropriate balance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sentimental treatment that creates sympathy for undeserving wrong-doer
rubrics_metrics.description: A danger in writing stories of crime lies in creating sympathy for the undeserving wrong-doer by a sentimental treatment of him and his act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make more or less of a hero of the wrong-doer; avoid treatments that lead indiscriminating readers to regard him and his crime as not unworthy of emulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and accuracy over picturesqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a temptation in writing crime stories to sacrifice truth and accuracy of detail in order to secure greater picturesqueness or stronger dramatic situations; such treatment is an indefensible deviation from the fundamental duty of presenting the news fairly and accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never alter or embellish facts for dramatic effect; fidelity to the actual facts is paramount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence should derive from facts, not moralizing/editorializing
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever influence a story of crime may have on the reader should be the result of the reporter's selection and presentation of the actual facts. Moralizing or 'editorializing' concerning the facts is not only unnecessary but undesirable in news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the facts show the moral or social lesson; avoid inserting the reporter's own sermonizing or overt editorial comment in straight crime reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic narrative and vivid description only when true
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic narrative and vivid description, when true to the facts of the news, are both legitimate and commendable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confessions, interviews with witnesses and persons involved, and clues to identity to produce effective narration and description; ensure all dramatization is faithful to verified facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent point of view and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to keep consistently to one point of view in arranging and presenting the details, particularly in constructive stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a single coherent perspective so the reader is not confused about interpretation or emphasis; arrange facts to support that chosen constructive angle without lapsing into contradiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness to accused and proper legal phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Fairness requires that persons accused of wrongdoing as well as their accusers be given a hearing in news stories; a person accused of crime is not a criminal unless he has been convicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until conviction, describe persons as 'alleged' criminals or say they are 'charged' with the crime; provide accused parties an opportunity to respond or have their side presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sources and materials for narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Available material for making the narration and the description effective includes confessions, interviews with witnesses and persons involved, and clues to the identity of the perpetrator or to the solution of any mysterious phases of the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on primary materials (confessions, witness interviews, physical clues) to build an engaging but accurate narrative; corroborate where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential factual contents for police/crime stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Details of significance in police news and crime stories: (1) number of lives destroyed or endangered; (2) names of victims; (3) names of persons charged with the crime; (4) arrests of suspects and detention of witnesses; (5) clues to the identity of the perpetrators when these are not known; (6) causes, motives, and responsibility, known or conjectured; (7) amount and character of loss; (8) methods employed in commission of the crime; (9) measures to prevent similar crimes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these elements where relevant to give readers a complete and useful account; item (9) encourages reporting prevention measures and public-safety responses.
